title: Credibility of the measures to enhance the career perspectives and employability of the researcher and contribution to his/her skills development
content:
## 2.1 Credibility of the measures to enhance the career perspectives and employability of the researcher and contribution to his/her skills development

FIELDWISE is designed so that its scientific work programme and its career-development architecture are the same object seen from two sides: every advanced competence the research requires is also a competence the fellow needs in order to move to the next stage of an independent career. The action is a European Fellowship hosted by Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), with a six-month non-academic placement at AgroVIR, over a total duration of 30 months (24 months at the host, M1-M24, plus the placement, M25-M30). This structure is used deliberately to deliver the MSCA-PF expected outcome of an increased set of research and transferable skills leading to improved employability and career prospects within academia and beyond (EO-01), and to substantiate the corresponding impact of improved researcher employability and career mobility within and outside academia (EI-01).

### Starting point and target trajectory

The fellow, Dr. Rositsa Cholakova, is a plant physiologist whose foundation lies in agronomy, plant protection and plant physiology, combined with developing expertise in Earth observation, GIS and agricultural data science. The fellowship is deliberately positioned to convert this profile into a scarce and distinctive one. The intended career progression is explicit and staged: from Plant Physiologist/Agronomist, through EO/Geospatial Crop Scientist, to an Independent researcher in transferable agricultural intelligence. FIELDWISE addresses the precise competence gap that stands between these stages — Bayesian modelling, spatio-temporal AI, sensor transfer, uncertainty, domain adaptation and decision evaluation — so that the measures below are not generic training but are targeted at named, missing capabilities the fellow can identify in her own record.

### Specific measures to develop advanced research skills

The scientific programme equips the fellow with advanced competence in Bayesian and probabilistic modelling, uncertainty quantification, spatio-temporal validation, sensor-domain transfer, cross-country adaptation, operational AI evaluation, research-to-MVP translation, and IP and exploitation. These are acquired through supervised research practice on the project's own work packages rather than in the abstract: the prospective, uncertainty-aware prediction work develops the probabilistic-modelling and uncertainty competences; the temporal and cross-country transferability work develops the domain-adaptation and validation competences; and the operational-transfer work develops the decision-evaluation and research-to-MVP competences.

Skills development is genuinely bidirectional, which is the mechanism that makes it interdisciplinary rather than one-directional up-skilling. ELTE, through its remote-sensing group, transfers to the fellow geoinformatics, EO time-series analysis, optical/SAR integration, hyperspectral-to-multispectral transfer, spatio-temporal modelling, Bayesian hierarchical modelling, uncertainty quantification, transfer learning and domain adaptation, reproducible geospatial computation, research software and web deployment, and IP and research exploitation. The fellow transfers to ELTE plant physiology, horticultural crop science, plant protection and agronomy, water-stress experimentation, physiological phenotyping, hyperspectral field measurement and the biological interpretation of EO. The transfer therefore runs crop physiology and agronomy against geospatial and data science in both directions, which is exactly the international and interdisciplinary mind-set the call seeks to forge.

### The Career Development Plan as the governing instrument

The measures are made operational, auditable and time-bound through a Career Development Plan, submitted as deliverable D1.3 Career Development Plan and established jointly by the supervisors and the researcher, consistent with the call requirement that such a plan be agreed jointly and submitted early in the action. With a co-supervisor in place, joint establishment is taken to mean that the plan is signed by both supervisors and the fellow. The plan comprises six components: research objectives (O1 to O6); training and career needs; transferable skills; teaching; publications planning; and open-science engagement. Its progress is tracked as a measurable indicator — the plan is agreed by M3 and reviewed at all five steering points (M6, M12, M16, M20 and M27) — so that career development is monitored on the same cadence as the science, including a review point inside the placement window when non-academic career development is most in play.

The transferable-skills strand is concrete and mapped to the call's training obligations: research integrity; open science and FAIR practice; generative-AI literacy; grant writing; IP and exploitation; project management; and science communication. These directly answer the requirement that fellowship training integrate key transferable and digital skills (including generative AI), Open Science culture, knowledge valorisation and research integrity. Discipline-specific competences are delivered as eleven structured ELTE-to-fellow competences, provided through supervised practice supported by named ELTE courses rather than left to osmosis. The quality and intensity of supervision underpinning this are specified: a weekly one-to-one meeting between the fellow and supervisor Prof. András Jung; a weekly technical session with co-supervisor Dr. Roland Hollós through WP3 and WP4, who provides the methodological lead and quality assurance for model development while the fellow designs, builds and runs the models; a monthly written progress record held by the fellow; and a quarterly review against the Career Development Plan attended by both supervisors.

### Measures to enhance employability outside academia — the non-academic placement

The single strongest employability measure is the six-month non-academic placement at AgroVIR (M25-M30), which supplies the inter-sectoral half of the career progression that the academic host structurally cannot provide: operational AI evaluation, research-to-MVP translation, and direct exposure to commercial agricultural-software requirements. The placement is inside the company that operates the farms and the FMIS, so the fellow acquires these competences in the environment where they are actually exercised — the nine-dimension MVP assessment, farmer-field access and the FMIS integration roadmap all depend on the company's own operational and customer-facing setting. On-site supervision during the placement is provided by Miklós Maróti at senior research grade, and the fellow is embedded in the AgroVIR product development team responsible for the FMIS platform, so that the placement is a supervised research-training period and not an unstructured secondment. This is the segment of the profile that makes the fellow employable in precision-agriculture, irrigation-technology and farm-management-information-system providers as well as in academia, and it lets her demonstrate, on the record, that she has taken a scientific concept through the full chain from experimental evidence to validated model, to cross-country testing, to commercial-field testing, and to a working MVP — an end-to-end delivery experience that few academic-only postdoctoral profiles can claim.

### Teaching, networking and public-engagement measures

The plan builds a teaching and supervision record appropriate to an independent-researcher trajectory: the fellow co-designs and delivers a full module unit within an ELTE MSc course on Earth observation for agriculture, rather than a single guest lecture, and co-supervises the field-experiment component of one PhD student's work. This is framed honestly as an existing strength transferred into a new setting rather than a competence acquired from zero: the fellow taught for five years at Agricultural University Plovdiv (2015-2020), including syllabus design, lecturing and examining in Bulgarian and English and Bachelor's thesis supervision, and the developmental content is the move to Earth-observation teaching in English at a Hungarian informatics faculty and the step up towards doctoral-level supervision. Networking and communication competences are developed through a defined publication programme (scientific outputs P1 to P4, with at least two high-quality peer-reviewed submissions during or shortly after the fellowship) and through public engagement beyond scientific peers, comprising one public field demonstration with AgroVIR farmers and one public-facing article per year, with science communication carried as one of the seven transferable-skill strands.

### Expected contribution to the future career of the researcher

Taken together, these measures create a distinctive scientific profile that combines biological understanding with scalable geospatial prediction and operational agricultural decision support — a combination that is uncommon precisely because it spans the physiology, the remote sensing and the deployment engineering that are usually held by different people. This profile is relevant to, and marketable across, European research institutes, universities, EU agricultural and environmental research, Earth-observation organisations, precision-agriculture companies, irrigation-technology providers and FMIS providers. The intended endpoint is the capacity for independent research in transferable agricultural intelligence, carried by an agreed and reviewed Career Development Plan; this is the researcher-level outcome the project commits to (OC6), and it is the concrete route by which FIELDWISE turns two years of research plus a six-month inter-sectoral placement into durably improved employability and career perspectives inside and outside academia.
